tier_reason: Methodology is A-grade (src/leibniz.f90 and src/leibniz.c at source revision c71e4cd, compile commands, compiler versions and the AMD EPYC-Genoa CPU are all in docs/history/2026-09-05T193245/raw/*.json), but no mechanism is stated or readable from the sources: the gap over gcc-built C coincides with source-form and flag differences (hand-unrolled Fortran loop, -Ofast vs -O3 plus three relaxed-math flags, gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0) and the lead over the clang builds is inside the three-sample range, so the wave-14 no-mechanism cap holds it at C.

corrections.workload: Single-threaded Leibniz series for pi, 1,000,000,000 terms per run (rounds.txt), timed with hyperfine; this historical run used two warm-up executions, three measured samples (TimesPerRun in the raw JSON) and a separate output execution; median wall time reported. Sources at revision c71e4cd81464b238172605982806c5bf827a70a1 (src/leibniz.f90, src/leibniz.c, src/leibniz.cpp).
corrections.caveats: Evidence would qualify as A (code, compiler versions, flags and CPU model are all public for both sides) but no mechanism is established, so the tier is capped at C. The margin over the best C/C++ build (clang++ 143.32 ms) is about 1% and inside the three-sample ranges; the suite's README warns that three samples cannot establish a winner for small differences. Flags are not matched: gfortran is built with -Ofast -ffast-math (adds -freciprocal-math, -ffinite-math-only, -fno-math-errno) while C sets only -fno-signed-zeros -fno-trapping-math -fassociative-math, and the backends differ (gfortran 14.3.0 vs gcc 15.2.0). The sources are not line-for-line equivalent: the Fortran loop is hand-unrolled by four with compile-time signs (do i=1,rounds,4: pi = pi + x/(2i+1) - x/(2i+3) + x/(2i+5) - x/(2i+7), signed 32-bit counter), while the C and C++ loops compute each term's sign from the index parity (x = -1.0 + 2.0*(i & 1)) in unsigned arithmetic; both sum the same 1e9 terms with one division each. The CalculatedPi values differ by about 1.5e-10 (Fortran 3.141592654730, C 3.1415926545850823), so the lower accuracy column (9.440 vs 9.499 digits) reflects both the 12-digit printout and a different summation order. Nim (142.43 ms), Rust SIMD (141.31 ms) and Objective-C (142.95 ms) are also faster than gcc C in the same snapshot; Nim compiles through gcc, so that gap comes from source form, not language. Explicit-SIMD C++ (AVX2) is slower (290.67 ms). In the earlier snapshot docs/history/2025-12-14T070941 (gfortran 14.2.0) Fortran took 238.94 ms: about 1.06x faster than C (gcc) 253.23 ms (derived from page data) but slower than C++ (clang++) 223.89 ms and C++ (g++) 226.37 ms and level with C (clang) 237.46 ms, so only the lead over gcc-built C is repeatable, and in that snapshot g++-built C++ beat gcc-built C by 1.12x on the same loop, which shows how much of the gap is run-to-run and build variation. The HEAD pipeline pins different compiler versions than the snapshot (not re-checked); the snapshot's per-target JSON was used here.
corrections.why_faster: Not established by the suite. From the sources the likely causes are not language properties: the Fortran loop is hand-unrolled by four with constant signs (no per-term parity-to-sign arithmetic), it is built with -Ofast/-ffast-math against narrower relaxed-math flags on the C side, and gfortran 14.3.0 is a different GCC backend than gcc 15.2.0. Against clang-built C/C++ the gap (1-3%) is within noise.

notes: Numbers match combined_results.csv and the per-target raw JSON exactly (Fortran 141.67 ms, C gcc 157.9, C++ g++ 158.78, C clang 146.07, C++ clang++ 143.32); earlier-snapshot figures also match. Shortcomings to record: no mechanism; flags not matched (-Ofast vs -O3 plus partial relaxed math); Fortran source hand-unrolled by four with constant signs vs per-term parity sign in C; lead over clang builds within three-sample noise; only the lead over gcc C repeats across snapshots; different summation result (CalculatedPi differs by 1.5e-10). Nim emits C, so the gap is Nim-generated C versus hand-written C compiled by the same clang. The Nim source matches the C source loop for loop, except that Nim's int arrays are 64-bit where C uses 32-bit int.
